subject: Environment
topic: Nuclear waste and radiation safety — mixed tiers
description: Categories of waste, AERB, IAEA, accidents, India's safeguards

questions.stem: Nuclear waste in India is regulated and overseen by:

options.option_text: BARC alone
Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB)
DRDO
ISRO

questions.explanation: AERB — set up 1983 under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962. Reports to the Atomic Energy Commission. Regulates safety in radiation, nuclear material, plant operation. Does the licensing of nuclear power plants, hospitals using radioisotopes, industrial radiography. Headquartered at Mumbai. India is also a signatory to IAEA conventions on nuclear safety, on the safety of spent fuel and radioactive waste.

questions.stem: Nuclear waste is typically classified by activity level into:

options.option_text: Liquid and Solid
Low-Level (LLW), Intermediate-Level (ILW), High-Level Waste (HLW)
Industrial and Domestic
Heavy and Light

questions.explanation: IAEA classification by activity / longevity: LLW — gloves, paper, gowns, mops; bury in shallow trenches. ILW — resins, sludges; needs shielding, often vitrified. HLW — spent fuel + reprocessing wastes; needs cooling for years, then deep geological disposal. India treats LLW + ILW at Trombay/Tarapur waste-management plants; HLW vitrified into borosilicate glass at Tarapur (since 1985), Trombay, Kalpakkam — first deep repository being planned (Onkalo in Finland is the world's first operational HLW repository).

Ukraine (then part of USSR)
Belarus
Lithuania

questions.explanation: Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant — situated in northern Ukraine (then a Soviet republic). Reactor 4 exploded on 26 April 1986 during a flawed safety test. Steam explosion + graphite fire released ~400× more radioactive material than Hiroshima. INES Level 7 (max). 30 km Exclusion Zone created. Belarus and Ukraine bore the brunt of fallout. Modern day: 'New Safe Confinement' shelter completed 2019. Same INES-7 rating: Fukushima Daiichi (March 2011, Japan) — but smaller release.

questions.stem: The 'INES' scale used to rate nuclear and radiological events ranges from:

options.option_text: 0-7 (Anomaly to Major Accident)

questions.explanation: INES — International Nuclear and Radiological Event Scale, developed by IAEA in 1990. 0 (deviation, no safety significance) up to 7 (major accident — large release of radioactive material). Each step = ~10× more severe. Levels 1-3 are 'incidents'; 4-7 are 'accidents'. Two Level-7 events in history — Chernobyl (1986), Fukushima Daiichi (2011). Three Mile Island (US, 1979) was Level 5. India's worst registered event — Kakrapar 2016 small heavy-water leak (INES Level 1).

questions.stem: The unit used for measuring the absorbed dose of ionising radiation in tissue is:

options.option_text: Becquerel (Bq)
Gray (Gy) for absorbed dose; Sievert (Sv) for biological-effect dose
Curie (Ci)
Roentgen (R)

questions.explanation: Three different concepts: ACTIVITY of source — Becquerel (Bq, decays/sec), older unit Curie (1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq). ABSORBED dose — Gray (Gy, 1 J/kg of tissue). EQUIVALENT / EFFECTIVE dose (biological-effect adjusted) — Sievert (Sv) = Gy × radiation weighting factor (1 for X/γ/β, 20 for α). Annual background dose ~3 mSv globally; ~6 mSv near Kerala/Tamil Nadu monazite beaches. CT scan — ~10 mSv. Lethal dose for ~50% of humans — ~4-5 Sv (LD50/30).

questions.stem: Vitrification of high-level nuclear waste is the process of:

options.option_text: Diluting the waste in water
Immobilising the waste in a stable borosilicate glass matrix for long-term storage
Burning the waste at high temperature
Re-enriching it for fuel

questions.explanation: Vitrification — HLW liquid is mixed with glass formers (silica, boron oxide, sodium oxide) and melted at ~1,150 °C, then cast into stainless steel canisters. The glass form has very low solubility — radionuclides immobilised for thousands of years. India has Waste Immobilisation Plants (WIPs) at Tarapur, Trombay, Kalpakkam. After vitrification, canisters go to interim storage; final disposal in deep geological repository (DGR). Bhabha Atomic Research Centre developed indigenous melter technology.

questions.stem: The IAEA — the global watchdog for atomic energy — was established in:

options.option_text: 1945, immediately after WWII
1957 — pursuant to Eisenhower's 'Atoms for Peace' speech (1953)
1968 — alongside NPT
1986 — after Chernobyl

questions.explanation: IAEA — International Atomic Energy Agency — formed 29 July 1957, headquartered in Vienna. Inspired by US President Eisenhower's 'Atoms for Peace' speech to the UN General Assembly (8 December 1953). Mission — promote peaceful use, ensure non-diversion to military use. Independent intergovernmental organisation, reports to both UNGA and UNSC. Awarded Nobel Peace Prize (2005, with Mohamed ElBaradei). Current Director General (since 2019) — Rafael Grossi (Argentina). India is a member.

questions.stem: Which type of ionising radiation is stopped completely by a single sheet of paper yet has the highest ionising power per unit path length?

options.option_text: Beta particles — negatively charged high-energy electrons
Alpha particles — helium-4 nuclei carrying two protons each
Gamma rays — high-energy electromagnetic photon radiation
Neutron radiation — uncharged particles released in fission

questions.explanation: Alpha particles (helium-4 nuclei) are the most densely ionising radiation but have the shortest range — stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper. Beta particles need millimetres of aluminium; gamma rays require centimetres of lead or concrete. Alpha particles are most dangerous if inhaled or ingested, not from external exposure.

questions.stem: The SI unit 'Becquerel' (Bq) quantifies which fundamental property of a radioactive substance?

options.option_text: Absorbed dose of radiation deposited in biological tissue
Biological effectiveness of a particular radiation type
Activity — the number of nuclear disintegrations per second
Equivalent dose received by a specific human organ or tissue

questions.explanation: One Becquerel = one radioactive decay event per second; it measures how active a sample is, not the biological harm caused. The Gray (Gy) measures absorbed dose; the Sievert (Sv) measures equivalent/effective dose accounting for biological impact. The older unit for activity was the Curie (Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq).

questions.stem: The radiation protection philosophy 'ALARA', mandated by India's Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) across all nuclear facilities, is an acronym for?

options.option_text: Atomic Level Absorption and Radiation Assessment standard
As Low As Reasonably Achievable in all radiation exposures
Allowable Limit for Annual Radiation in the Atmosphere
Authorized Limit for Absorbed Radiation Activity threshold

questions.explanation: ALARA — As Low As Reasonably Achievable — requires radiation workers and facilities to keep exposures well below regulatory dose limits using three key tools: minimising time of exposure, maximising distance from the source, and using adequate shielding. Options A, C, and D are plausible-sounding but fabricated expansions of the acronym.

questions.stem: 'Deep Geological Disposal' (DGD), involving placement of waste in stable rock formations 300–1000 m underground, is the internationally endorsed permanent strategy for which waste category?

options.option_text: Low-level waste generated by hospital radiotherapy and diagnostics
Very-low-level waste from decommissioned nuclear power plant tools
High-level waste from spent fuel with half-lives up to 24,000 years
Intermediate-level waste from reactor coolant and ion-exchange resins

questions.explanation: High-level waste (HLW) contains long-lived radionuclides such as Plutonium-239 (half-life ~24,000 years) requiring isolation over geological timescales. DGD in stable granite or clay is the consensus solution. Finland's Onkalo repository is the world's first operational HLW DGD facility. Low-level and very-low-level waste are managed in near-surface engineered repositories.

questions.stem: Emergency responders distribute potassium iodide (KI) tablets to populations near nuclear accident sites. Which radioactive fission product does KI specifically protect against, and why?

options.option_text: Caesium-137 — a gamma emitter with a 30-year environmental half-life
Strontium-90 — a beta emitter that chemically mimics calcium in bones
Iodine-131 — a beta/gamma emitter concentrated by the thyroid gland
Plutonium-239 — a long-lived alpha emitter present in spent reactor fuel

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland absorbs dietary iodine to produce hormones and cannot distinguish stable I-127 from radioactive I-131. Pre-loading the thyroid with stable KI saturates its uptake capacity, blocking I-131 absorption. Cs-137 and Sr-90 are also major fission products but have no equivalent targeted countermeasure; Pu-239 is an alpha emitter with a different exposure pathway.

questions.stem: The 2011 Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster differed fundamentally from Chernobyl in its root cause. What primarily triggered the three reactor core meltdowns at Fukushima?

options.option_text: A runaway chain reaction caused by an inherent RBMK reactor design flaw
Station blackout after a tsunami inundated and destroyed diesel generators
Operator error during a scheduled low-power reactor safety test exercise
Hydrogen ignition inside the primary containment vessel during refuelling

questions.explanation: The March 2011 Tōhoku tsunami, triggered by a magnitude-9.0 earthquake, flooded the Fukushima Daiichi site and disabled 12 of 13 backup diesel generators, causing a prolonged station blackout. Without coolant circulation, three cores melted within days. Options A and C describe Chernobyl's root causes — the positive void coefficient of the RBMK reactor and operator error during a safety test — making them the most tempting wrong answers.

questions.stem: India's three-stage nuclear programme centres on converting fertile Thorium-232 into a fissile material usable as reactor fuel. Which fissile isotope is produced through this process?

options.option_text: Uranium-235 — a naturally fissile isotope requiring centrifuge enrichment
Plutonium-239 — bred when U-238 absorbs a neutron in a fast reactor
Uranium-233 — bred when Th-232 absorbs a neutron and beta-decays twice
Curium-245 — a transuranic actinide recovered from spent fuel reprocessing

questions.explanation: Th-232 is fertile, not fissile. On neutron absorption it becomes Th-233, which beta-decays to Protactinium-233 (Pa-233), then beta-decays again to Uranium-233 — a fissile isotope. India holds the world's largest thorium reserves (~25% globally), making Stage 3 of the nuclear programme strategically critical. Option B (Pu-239) describes the Stage 2 product from U-238 in fast breeder reactors, not from thorium.
